analysis.investment_thesis: Jayaswal Neco is a heavily indebted commodity steel producer with collapsing earnings — net profit has crashed 95% from ₹2,247 Cr (2022 supercycle windfall) to just ₹113 Cr in 2025, with finance costs of ₹554 Cr consuming 58% of EBITDA. There is no moat, no growth, and negative ROE — this is not an India compounding story, it is a debt-restructuring survivor.
key_strengths: Debt reduction happening — total debt down from ₹3,845 Cr (2022) to ₹2,753 Cr (2025), directionally positive
Strong OCF recovery — ₹1,388 Cr in FY25 and FCF of ₹1,144 Cr shows operational cash generation
Diversified end-markets — automotive, railways, defence, infrastructure castings provide some revenue stability
key_risks: Finance cost of ₹554 Cr in FY25 is strangling equity returns — at EBITDA of ₹947 Cr, interest coverage is a thin 1.7x
Zero revenue growth — flat between ₹5,926–6,332 Cr for four years with no visible catalyst
Commodity steel with no pricing power — margins are entirely at the mercy of global iron ore and steel price cycles
red_flags: ROE of -0.87% and ROCE of 2.93% — both well below cost of capital; the business is destroying equity value
Historical capital misallocation — borrowings exploded from ₹1,244 Cr (2011) to ₹4,114 Cr (2016) with CWIP of ₹3,163 Cr, signalling reckless capex cycles
Stated P/E of 25x is dangerously misleading — at current net profit of ₹113 Cr vs market cap of ₹9,345 Cr, the true earnings multiple is ~83x for a no-moat steel company
Near-zero institutional interest: FII at 0.90%, DII at 0.30% — smart money is absent
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Bhai, this is a commodity steel company that had one exceptional year (FY22 post-COVID steel supercycle, ₹2,247 Cr profit) and the market seems to be still pricing in that peak. The reality in FY25 is brutal — net profit of just ₹113 Cr on revenues of ₹5,985 Cr, which means the actual P/E is ~83x, not the 25x headline figure. With ₹554 Cr in annual finance costs devouring the bulk of EBITDA, this is essentially a lender-owned business that equity holders are praying for. ROCE of 2.93% tells me every rupee of capital employed is earning nothing above treasury rates. I would never pay 3.6x book for this.

The historical record is damning — management destroyed capital from 2011 to 2016, growing debt from ₹1,244 Cr to ₹4,114 Cr while CWIP ballooned to ₹3,163 Cr with no commensurate revenue growth. That is not the promoter quality I demand. The only silver lining is active debt reduction (₹1,092 Cr reduced in 3 years) and strong operating cash flows in FY25, but this recovery is fragile and entirely dependent on steel spreads staying supportive. India's infrastructure boom will help the sector broadly, but I want to own the best-in-class — JSW Steel, SAIL at the right price — not a leveraged mid-tier operator with unproven capital discipline. Hard pass.
